*Ritter*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German ritter,from Middle Dutch ridder,Flemish byform of from Middle Dutch rîder,from Middle Dutch rîden+from Middle Dutch -er (equivalent to German reiten+-er).}In Middle High German,both from Middle High German ritter and from Middle High German rīter (whence modern from German notext1) were used in the sense of “horseman”,“mounted man-at-arms”,as well as for the (emerging) rank of “knight”,and,by generalisation,any member of the lower nobility. Gradually,both forms were separated semantically (a vocabulary of 1487 has two distinct entries:''miles:ritter'' vs. ''equester:reitter''),and in early modern German a third (similar,though unrelated) form Reuter,from Dutch,was introduced. In this period,''@^'' was the term for the class of the German lower nobility,''Reuter'' was the normal word for a cavalryman,and ''Reiter'' was rare but sometimes used for “horseman”. From the 18th century,was gradually replaced by Kavalier,especially with individual noblemen,whereas the collective @^schaft remained in use for the class as a whole. Accordingly,becomes increasingly limited to the historic or romantic/poetic “medieval knight”.|Pronunciation}/ˈʁɪtɐ/}Ⓓ/9/9a/De-@^.ogg(Germany)(Germany)}Ⓓ/e/ef/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)|Noun}(mask.)}#knight}#}• Endlich erschien eines Tages ein wohlgewappneter '''@^''' und schwor  dass er den Kampf mit dem Drachen aufnehmen wolle. (Finally one day a well-armed '''knight''' appeared)  who swore that he would take up arms against the dragon.|Derived terms}Deutschordensritter}Deutschritter}Grabesritter}Gralsritter}Glücksritter}Jediritter,Jedi-@^}Johanniterritter,Johanniter-@^}Kolumbusritter,Kolumbus-@^}Konjunkturritter}Kreuzritter}Malteserritter,Malteser-@^}Minneritter}Ordensritter}Privilegienritter}Raubritter}Reichsritter}Reichsritteraufstand}@^akademie}@^anolis}@^aufstand}@^bank}@^bund}@^burg}@^dichtung}@^dienst}@^drama}@^essen}@^falter}@^festspiel}@^frau}@^fräulein}@^geschichte}@^gewand}@^grundel}@^gut}@^gutsbesitzer}ritterhaft}@^haftigkeit}@^in}@^kampf}@^kampfspiel}@^kreuz}@^kreuzträger}@^krieg}@^lehen}ritterlich}@^ling}rittern}@^ ohne Furcht und Tadel}@^orden}@^roman}@^runde}@^rüstung}@^saal}@^schaft}ritterschaftlich}@^schlag}@^schwert}@^sfrau}@^sitz}@^smann}@^spiel}@^sporn}@^stand}@^stern}@^steuer}@^straße}@^stück}@^tafel}@^taube}@^tum}@^-und-Räuber-Roman}@^wanze}@^wesen}@^würde}@^zeit}@^zug}Römerritter}Strauchritter}Tempelritter}Arme @^|Proper noun}surname)}#surname

*-s*German{}|Etymology 1}from Middle High German -es,from German goh.|Alternative forms}-es}proper nouns ending with a sibilant consonant; dated}proper nouns ending with a sibilant consonant}common nouns; now proscribed}proper nouns; correct in certain cases,but often seen as a misspelling|Suffix}#used to form the genitive singular of most masculine nouns,neuter nouns,and proper nouns of all genders|Usage notes}The formation of the strong genitive singular (in ''&_,-es'',or no ending) may be of some difficulty both for learners and native speakers.}Only one form is possible in some nouns:}Nouns in unstressed ''-as,-es,- is,-os,-us'' remain unchanged (except those in -nis,which make ''-nisses'').}Other nouns in ''&_,-ß,-x,-z'' take ''-es''.}Nouns ending in a vowel or in unstressed ''-el,-em,-en,-er,-or,-um'' take ''&_''. (Only those in a diphthong or in ''-h'' allow ''-es'',alternatively.)}Nouns forming their plural in ''&_'' take the same ending also in the genitive singular. (Apparent exceptions will generally have an alternative plural in ''-e''.)}Otherwise,both forms are usually correct,but certain tendencies can be observed:}The ''es''-form is strongly preferred in a number of frequently used monosyllables,to the degree that the ''s''-form may even sound odd. No hard rule can be given to identify these nouns; they include e.g. Land,Mann,Weg,etc.}The ''es''-form is also preferred,for euphonic reasons,in words ending in certain clusters like ''-pf,&_ch,&_t''.}Most other monosyllables have no clear preference.}The ''s''-form is usually preferred in polysyllables,regardless of their being simple or compound and regardless also of stress patterns.}Note,finally,that there is a fairly strong tendency for proper nouns (used with the article) and for newer or less common loanwords to remain unchanged in the genitive singular.|Etymology 2}Probably derived from the genitive ''&_'' (etymology 1),but developed into a noun-forming suffix in from German Low German - and Central German dialects.|Suffix}#used to form nouns from verb stems}•klacken}•schnappen|Etymology 3}Borrowed gml. Reinforced by the fact that from French - and English - also use ''&_'' as a plural suffix.|Alternative forms}now proscribed}family names ending with a sibilant consonant|Suffix}#Used to form the plurals of some nouns.}#Used to form the plurals of personal names,particularly family names.|Usage notes}The plural ending ''&_'' is most typical of loanwords (as in Schals,Parfüms,Videos),though there is a tendency for naturalised loanwords to switch to -e or -en (compare Generäle,Lifte,Pizzen with older Generals,Lifts,Pizzas). Conversely,''&_'' is also used in a certain number of native words (as in Fräuleins,Mädels,Uhus). Moreover,it is the most productive plural marker in contemporary German,typically used to pluralise initialisms (LKWs),neologisms (Honks),and words that do not otherwise have a common plural form (Streits).|Suffix}#Used to form adverbs from substantives:}•der Tag}•die Nacht}•die Linke}•der Anfang}#Sometimes used to form adverbs from adjectivess:}•bereit}•beiderrseitig|See also}&_-||Low German{}|Etymology}gml,from from Old Saxon -es,the masculine and neuter genitive singular ending of strong nouns.|Suffix}#archaic Used to form the genitive case of (strong) masculine and neuter nouns.}#rare Used to form the genitive case of proper nouns.}#Used to form the partitive form of the adjective}•groot → wat groot'''s'''}#Used to form adverbs}•Nacht → nachts
*S*German{}|Etymology}For the origin of the letter,see from Translingual s.}Orthography and pronunciation}&_ingle ''s'' in prevocalic position is pronounced/z/,except when it follows an obstruent within the word stem (e.g. Achse,bugsieren,Lotse,schubsen)./s/is usually retained in recent borrowings from English (e.g. &_ex),to a lesser degree also in recent borrowings from other languages (e.g. &_alsa). Words from the classical languages and pre-1900 loanwords behave like native words.}&_tem-initial ''st'' and ''sp'' are pronounced/ʃt/and/ʃp/in native words. The same is generally true for classical and pre-1900 loanwords,though in this case we find some exceptions which are at least optionally pronounced with/sp/(e.g. &_til,&_tola). Recent borrowings tend to retain the original sounds. Again,this tendency is stronger with English than with other source languages (cf. e.g. &_paghetti with/ʃp/).}The trigraph ''sch'' is pronounced/ʃ/,except when there is an intervening morpheme boundary,which normally happens only with the diminutive suffix -chen (cf. e.g. Häuschen).}Otherwise,pre-consonantal and word-final ''s'' is always pronounced/s/. This also includes ''st,sp'' when they are not stem-initial. The same is generally true for doubled ''ss''. There are,however,a few words in which ''ss'' may – optionally – be pronounced/z/(e.g. Fussel,Massel,quasseln,&_chussel). For the orthographic choice between ''ss'' and ß,see the latter.}{{rel-bottom|Pronunciation}q-lite:letter/ɛs/}De-&_.OGG}ess}q-lite:phoneme/z/q-lite:see etymology section|Letter}de-letter:scLatn}#Latn-def:es}#}&_ Für die zweierlei '''&_''',das scharfe ß und das weiche,tönende s,sind die Zeichen s und ſ zu empfehlen. Letzteres wird im Französischen,Englischen,Holländischen,Polnischen,Madjarischen mit z bezeichnet,das wir nicht annehmen können,weil bei uns,wie schon bemerkt,z den Laut ts bezeichnet.|Noun}#Abbreviation of [&_üd]; south

*Sal*German{}|Alternative forms}Sial|Etymology}in1909,in ''Das Antlitz der Erde'',as a nocap1.tWe further assume the existence of three zones or envelopes as determining the structure of the earth,namely,the barysphere or the Nife (Ni-Fe),Sima (Si-Mg),and '''&_''' (Si-Al). This division differs from the classification which has been proposed by distinguished American petrographers,in the separation of the metallic barysphere (Nife).|Noun}(neut.)}#geology The uppermost layer of the Earth,rich in silica- and alumina-bearing minerals.}#}• Wir nehmen ferner drei Zonen oder Hüllen als maassgebend für die Beschaffenheit der Erde an  u. zw. die Barysphäre oder das Nife (Ni-Fe)  ferner Sima (Si-Mg) und '''&_''' (Si-Al). Diese Theilung unterscheidet sich von der Classification  die von hervorragenden americanischen Petrographen vorgeschlagen wurde  durch die Abtrennung der metallischen Barysphäre (Nife). Compare from Dutch zat,from English sad,from Danish sat.|Pronunciation}/zat/}Ⓓ6/61/De-@^.ogg}Rhymes:at|Adjective}#not hungry,satiated,full,done}•Willst du noch was? − Nein danke,ich bin '''@^'''.}•Do you want some more? – No thanks,I'm done.}#fed up,sick of qualifier:see usage notes}•Ich habe deinen Quatsch '''@^'''!}•I'm '''sick of''' your nonsense!}#}@^ „Eine halbe Woche lang habe ich diesen Höllenlärm über mich ergehen lassen,dann bekam ich es '''@^'''!“}•For half a week I let this hellish noise go on above me,and then I got fed up with it!}#full,ample}#}• Sogar die Zahl der Millionäre wuchs 2009 um '''@^e''' 17 Prozent. Even rarer is use with ''sein'' and the genitive (''ich bin dieser Sache @^''/''ich bin seiner @^''),which was common in the 1800s and earlier and which is marked as literary by the ''Duden'' and ''DWDS'' but is now very rare even in books (except in the expression ''des Lebens @^ sein'',for example,which is used in the Bible and probably therefore continues to be used in books,though ''das Leben @^ sein'' has become as common in books since about 1890).

*Schach*German{}|Etymology}from Proto-Indo-European ⋆tek-}From Middle High German schāch,from Arabic شاه,from tršāh,from scPhli,from scXpeo. Scheck.}Oriental words were usually borrowed into Middle High German through Italian or Old French. Therefore the final/x/is remarkable,because this sound was replaced with/k/in from Italian scacco,from Old French échec. There are two possible explanations for this:Either the word was borrowed directly from Arabic during the early Crusades,or it was borrowed through from Middle Dutch schaec and the ''-ch'' goes back to artificial reproduction of the High German consonant shift (as happened in several other words).|Pronunciation}/ʃax/}Ⓓ/8/8a/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)}Ⓓ1/16/De-@^.ogg}Rhymes:ax|Noun}(neut.,plural:[@^s])}#chess Literally:[game]}#check Literally:[chess situation in which the king is directly threatened]|Derived terms}Blitzschach}Damenschach}Dauerschach}Doppelschach}Reiseschach}Schnellschach}Simultanschach}Steckschach}Vierschach}@^anleitung}@^aufgabe}@^brett}@^buch}@^club}@^fibel}@^figur}@^gebot}@^genie}@^großmeister}@^klub}@^länderkampf}@^mannschaft}Schmachmatt}schachmatt}@^meister}@^meisterschaft}@^olympiade}@^partie}@^problem}@^spiel}@^spieler}@^sport}@^tisch}@^turnier}@^uhr}@^weltmeister}@^weltmeisterschaft}@^wettkampf}@^zug|Descendants}desctree:шах}desctree:schack|Noun}(mask.,plural:[@^s][s][e])}#Schah

*Schauwecker*German{}|Etymology}A German surname originating in the city of Reutlingen,from 'schauen' meaning 'to look' or 'to keep watch' and 'wecken'+-er,'one who alerts' or 'raises the alarm'. The name thus denotes the duties of a sentinel,and dates back to the fortification of the city in the early 13th century.|Proper noun}surname)}#surname

*schiech*German{}|Alternative forms}schiach|Etymology}From Middle High German @^,from Old High German ⋆skioh,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆skeuh. from German scheu. Compare from Bavarian schiach.|Pronunciation}/ʃiːç/,(standard)}/ʃɪɐ̯x/,(Bavarian)|Adjective}#colloquial ugly}#colloquial angry|Usage notes}The word is common in Bavaria and Austria,but is mostly confined to oral conversation in the local Bavarian dialects,where it would typically be pronounced ic:ʃɪɐ̯x. Since the word only rarely appears in written form,and the dialectal ɪɐ̯ diphthong very often corresponds to ic:iʁ or ic:iːʁ in the standard language,some speakers hypercorrectly pronounce the word ic:ʃɪʁç and spell it ''schirch'' when using it in the context of Standard German.

*schief*German{}|Etymology}From northern from Middle High German @^,from Middle High German schīf (etc.),from Middle Low German schêf,from Old Saxon ⋆skêf,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆skaib,from Proto-Germanic ⋆skaibaz.}Regular High German cognates exist only in north-western Central German; compare from Central Franconian scheif,northernmost from Luxembourgish scheef. *schlagfertig*German{}|Etymology}Mid-17th century, equivalent to Schlag,fertig,(hit) blow,(ready) capable. Probably a from Dutch nocap1. For this speak the slightly earlier attestion (1625),the invariably nautical context of the earliest German attestations,and the fact that from Dutch slag means “battle”. This is how it stands with the selling of cars,where this formula is good and useful,but also with the “selling of religion” and the “selling of education”. Always the offered – economical or spiritual – commodity has to be cheap,accessible to the last one in the mass.

*schlecht*German{}|Etymology}From earlier slecht,from Middle High German sleht,from Old High German sleht (see also schlicht),from Proto-Germanic ⋆slihtaz. Cognate with from English slight,from Dutch slecht,from Afrikaans sleg,from Icelandic sléttur,from Faroese slættur,from Swedish slätt,from Danish slet ,from Gothic 𐍃𐌻𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍄𐍃,and from Norwegian slett.|Pronunciation}/ʃlɛçt/}Rhymes:ɛçt}Ⓓb/b4/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ9/90/De-@^2.ogg}Ⓓ/a/a1/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)|Adjective}#bad,evil,wicked Literally:[the opposite of good; immoral]}•ein '''@^er''' Mensch}•a '''bad''' person}#bad Literally:[unskilled; of limited ability]}•sie ist '''@^''' in Mathe}•she is '''bad''' at maths}#bad Literally:[unhealthy,unwell]}•'''@^''' für jemanden sein}•to be '''bad''' for someone}#bad Literally:[of poor physical appearance]}•'''@^''' aussehen}•to look '''bad'''}#bad,off Literally:[spoiled,rotten,overripe]}•'''@^''' werden}•to go '''off''',to go '''bad'''}#dirty Literally:[dishonourable]|Usage notes}@^ and schlimm could be considered synonyms,but there is a difference in connotation. Use @^ for "bad" in situations where judgment is involved,implying a certain level of objectivity ("bad job,bad idea,bad manners,bad quality").}Use schlimm to mean "bad" when a negative consequence is implied and it negatively affects a person or creature ("bad accident,bad cold,bad injury").}Sometimes you can use either word. For example,you could say "@^er Traum" or "schlimmer Traum" for 'bad dream'. The connotation of using "@^er" would imply the 'bad dream' wasn't that harmful after waking up (like,'it was just a bad dream. I'm fine.'); whereas,using "schlimmer" would imply that the 'bad dream' had a lasting impact even after waking up,kind of like saying 'awful dream'. Same with "@^er Tag" and "schlimmer Tag" ('bad day'). "schlimmer Tag" would be closer to 'awful day' in the sense that it implies the negative consequences of the bad day will carry over to tomorrow.|Derived terms}einen @^en Tag haben}@^hin}S1-Ĭigkeit}@^machen}S1-Ĭsein}ver@^ern|Adverb}#badly,poorly,not well Literally:[in a bad or poor manner]}#with difficulty,not easily|See also}schlimm}übel}böse||Pennsylvania German{}|Etymology}Compare from German @^,from Dutch slecht.|Adjective}#bad}#wicked|Adverb}#poorly

*schlecken*German{}|Pronunciation}/ˈʃlɛ.kən/,(standard)}/ˈʃlɛ.ʔŋ̩/,(commonly)}Ⓓ4/4b/De-@^.ogg|Verb}#to lick,to lap|Usage notes}While this word is more common in the south,and even the standard word for ''to lick'' in many Swiss dialects,in the north it is exclusively associated with the consumption of sweets such as lollipops and ice cream or the consumption of milk by cats. But even in these cases it is used rather rarely. It should hence be avoided in formal conversation in favor of ''lecken'',as it is likely to be perceived as queer or childish by people whose speech doesn't commonly include it.

The elimination of this '''litherness''' I will not be an observer of in my lifetime  even if Plato himself were to rise from his ashes and teach the pedants the right pronunciation. *schlicht*German{}|Pronunciation}/ʃlɪçt/}Ⓓ3/32/De-@^.ogg}Rhymes:ɪçt|Etymology 1}Chiefly Low German,also to a lesser degree Central German variant of from German notext1. From Middle Low German slicht and northern from Middle High German sliht (both “flat,straight,simple”),from Proto-Germanic ⋆slihtaz,which see for cognates. Since the Late Middle Ages,developed the sense “bad”,which became predominant over time,but did not displace the original one entirely. By the 17th century,attempts were made to reserve the ''i''-variant specifically to the older meaning,but the semantic split between both forms was completed only during the 19th century. The adverbs schlechthin and schlechterdings (both “plainly,absolutely”) remain as relicts to this day.|Adjective}#plain,simple,artless,natural|Derived terms}@^en}S1-Ĭheit|Etymology 2}nonlemma|Verb}#verb form of [schleichen]

Nichte). ''@-3ft'' pertains to the verb schliefen. This etymology is favoured by most authorities,although they seem to be unable to find attestations for the from Middle Low German - word.}There is an Upper German attestation of from Middle High German wazzersluht or possibly from Middle High German -slůht (“water-filled ditch”),which is in line with similar words in modern Upper German dialects. *schmeicheln*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German smeicheln,from Middle High German smeichelen,of from German nocap1 origin. Possibly an iterative of from Middle High German smeichen; or alternatively from Old High German ⋆smeihhalōn,from Proto-West Germanic tto caress,flatter,stroke,an iterative of from Proto-West Germanic ⋆smaikōn. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European ⋆smē(y)g-/from Proto-Indo-European ⋆smī̌g-,a guttural extension of from Proto-Indo-European ⋆smē-/from Proto-Indo-European tto smear,wipe over. Equivalent to schmeichen+-eln. Cognate with from German Low German tto coax,flatter,from Saterland Frisian tto flatter. *Schmelztopf*German{}|Etymology}schmelzen,Topf,(to melt)(pot)|Pronunciation}ˈʃmɛlt͡s.topf|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^ses,plural:[@^e])}#melting pot}#}@^ :A:pages206–207:Das Elend der Universitäten beginnt,wie wir sahen,schon bei den Grundschulen und High Schools. Diesen weist der Amerikanismus eine soziale Funktion zu,die alles andere überschattet:'''@^''' der Rassen zu sein und die Mentalität von Kindern,deren Eltern oder Großeltern nicht nur durch Erdteile,sondern durch Kultur,Sitten und Sprache getrennt lebten,der Einheitsforderung des Adoptivlandes zu unterwerfen. Während die rein erzieherischen Aufgaben naturgemäß zurückzutreten haben,wird das geistige Individuum bewußt auf die Normalformel gebracht.:The misery of the universities begins,as we have seen,already in the primary schools and high schools. To these the Americanism assigns the social function that overshadows all:Being a melting pot of all races and subordinating the mentality of children whose parents and grandparents have not been living separated by continents,but by culture,traditions and language,to the demand of oneness of the adoptive country. Whereas the educational tasks naturally have to step back,the mental individual is being brought intentionally to the formula of normality.

*Schreibe*German{}|Etymology}schreiben|Pronunciation}ˈʃʁaɪ̯bə}Ⓓ1/15/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(fem.)}#informal writing}#informal (writing) style}•synononym:@-1stil}•eine flotte '''@^'''}#}• Das zeitgenössische Gedicht hat andere Merkmale. Es erscheint oft wie reimlose Prosa  bevorzugt im Druckbild seine besondere optische Erscheinung  es bevorzugt das Wort als schwer zu enträtselnde Chiffre  es setzt die Reihung der Wörter und seine Wiederholung als Stilelement ein. Der prosaähnliche Vers ist aber von einem Atem-Rhythmus geprägt und verzichtet von daher auch oftmals auf die Zeichensetzung. Hinzu kommen die inhaltlich neuen Schwerpunkte. War es früher ein Rühmen und Preisen von Dingen und Welt  ist es heute das schlichte Sagen  ein banales Benennen  eine realistische '''@^'''  die sich kritisch und politisch gibt  was jeweils unter politisch verstanden wird. (The contemporary poem often has different characteristics. It often resembles rhymeless prose)  prefers a particular look in print  it prefers the word as a cipher hard to decipher  it employs the rowing of words and its repetition as a means of style. The prose-resembling verse however is characterized by a breath-rhythm und therefore often forgoes punctuation  too. In addition to that  there there are new topical focusses. *Schreibtisch*German{}with drawers}from German;schreiben,Tisch,|Pronunciation}/ˈʃʁaɪ̯pˌtɪʃ/}Ⓓf/fe/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ2/24/De-@^2.ogg}Rhymes:ɪʃ|Noun}(mask.,plural:[@^(e)s])}#desk,cabinet Literally:[any table,frame,or case for the use of writers and readers; also a place for storing the papers]|Usage notes}The term ''s1-Ĭ'' was used in 16th and 17th century for cabinets (in german Kabinett or Kabinettschrank). This naming comes from original purpose of cabinets used for writing and storing the papers,so called Bargueño desks). These cabinets were often provided with an openable front panel,used for writing,which hides several drawers for storing the papers or utentils inside. Bargueño desks were copied in other parts of Europe and produced in several forms. Many of them were not even equipped with the writing desk,however the term ''s1-Ĭ'' was used for them.|Derived terms}@^lampe}@^sessel}@^täter}@^verbrecher}@^verbrechen

*schummeln*German{}|Etymology}There are two main theories,which need not be mutually exclusive but may complement each other.}From dialectal ,originally probably “to move back and forth”,whence various attested senses:“waver,totter; rock,swing,push; chase off; abscond,steal away; take clandestinely; rummage; bustle about; do housework”,etc. In favour of this derivation speaks that the sense “to cheat” was sometimes associated with “trickery through swift movements”,especially in the context of gambling. The verb  (in the above-mentioned senses) is found in dialects as far south as Tyrol,but Adelung considered it chiefly Low German and the earliest attestations are of late from Middle Dutch scommelen (1410:“to do kitchenwork”,1530:“to rock,move back and forth”); hence probably of northern origin through from Middle Low German ⋆@-1en,eventually perhaps onomatopoeic. Compare modern from Dutch schommelen. Compare also from German tto cheat,from schaukeln.}Through a dialectally attested sense “to trade (of a Jewish merchant)”,from Yiddish שום,an acronym for the cities of Speyer,Worms,Mainz,the so-called Schum cities,old centres of Jewish religion and trade. However,a verb derived from this acronym is not attested in Yiddish and the sense “to trade” may be derived from the sense “to cheat”,rather than vice versa.|Pronunciation}/ˈʃʊməln/}Ⓓb/ba/De-@^.ogg}schum+meln|Verb}#intransitive to cheat Literally:[especially in games,but also in business,school,etc.]}•synononym:mogeln|Derived terms}S1-Ĭ,Schummler,Schummelei,Ge@-1,Schummel}@^d,ge@-1t}be@^,er@^

*Schuster, bleib bei deinem Leisten*German{}|Alternative forms}Schuster,bleib bei deinen Leisten|Pronunciation}/ˈʃuːstɐ blaɪ̯p baɪ̯ ˈdaɪ̯nəm ˈlaɪ̯stn̩/}Ⓓe/e2/De-Schuster%2C_bleib_bei_deinem_Leisten.ogg|Proverb}#cobbler,keep to your last gl:one should stick to what one knows and has experience with}#}• Dazu gibt es unzählige Beispiele. Mangelndes Wissen  unzureichende Sachkenntnis und falsche Informationen führen schnell zu Pleiten und Firmenzusammenbrüchen. (There are countless examples of this. The admonishing words “'''cobbler)  keep to your last!'''” therefore cannot be said often enough. Lacking knowledge  insufficient expertise and wrong information quickly lead to brankruptcies and company collapses.

*schwanen*German{}|Etymology}Sometimes taken as a loan from gml,but first attestations are nearly contemporaneous (1514 for Low German,1543 for High German,according to Grimm). Semantic derivation disputed. The ''Duden'' dictionary suspects a learned jocular translation from Latin from Latin tI smell something (with dative construction as in German),due to phonetic similarity of Latin from Latin tto smell and from Latin tswan. Grimm however,because of the early and near-contemporaneous attestations in different regions,sees it as an inherited word of the common people,connecting it to the traditional Germanic association of swans with prophecy and fate (cf. the Norns) and pointing to the synonymous expression . Earlier variants contain -d- (''@-2den'',from Low German swanden),probably under influence of ahnden,a once common variant of ahnen.|Pronunciation}/ˈʃvaːnən/}Ⓓc/c8/De-@^.ogg|Verb}#colloquial to anticipate (something bad),to suspect,to dread}•synononym:[ahnen],[befürchten]}•Mir '''@-2t''' nichts Gutes.}•I sense something bad coming up.}•litI anticipate nothing good.}#}• Ihm '''@-2te''' Übles bei seinem bevorstehenden Besuch im Polizeihauptquartier. Aber diesmal nicht aus den üblichen Gründen. Dieser eine Messerstich hatte ihm nicht nur einen Freund genommen  sondern auch gleich beide Stellungen.

*Sechtem*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German Sephteme,probably from Latin tseventh in a supposed from Latin tat the seventh league,the place being roughly seven Roman leagues (a bit over 15 km) away from Bonn. The sound shift ''pt'' → ''ft'' through Primärberührung,the further shift ''ft'' → ''cht'' through the northwestern,especially Dutch,development,which is amply attested in the Rhineland (cf. from Luxembourgish Griecht,from Luxembourgish Luucht,from Luxembourgish uechter).|Pronunciation}/ˈzɛçtəm/|Proper noun}#Place A village,officially a quarter of Bornheim,s/North Rhine-Westphalia,c/Germany.
